query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a dense, 1–2 µm Al2O3 overlayer on boride-based components via PVD or thermal spraying will significantly enhance their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion by serving as a stable diffusion barrier.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based substrates commonly used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
generation.intervention: Form a continuous, low-porosity Al2O3 coating (1–2 µm) on the boride substrate using PVD or thermal spray methods.
generation.conditions: Exposure to molten aluminum at typical hot-dip plating temperatures (approximately 660–750 °C) for extended service durations.
generation.structural_mediator: A thermally stable alumina overlayer preventing direct contact between the molten aluminum and the underlying boride material.
generation.mechanism: The oxide film acts as an effective diffusion barrier, limiting chemical reaction, interdiffusion, and dissolution of the boride substrate into molten aluminum.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to uncoated boride components, the coated samples exhibit measurably lower mass loss and a longer service lifetime under molten-aluminum exposure.
generation.baseline: Equivalent boride-based coupons without an Al2O3 overlayer, tested under the same molten-aluminum conditions.
generation.boundary: If flaws or pores exceed ~1% of the coating area, or if the operational temperature approaches or exceeds 800 °C or mechanical damage compromises the coating integrity, reduced protection may occur.
generation.uncertainty: Exact degree of improvement is not yet fully quantified under industrial conditions; interfacial adhesion and performance over very long exposures remain to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Expose matched sets of Al2O3-coated and uncoated boride coupons to a molten aluminum bath at 700−750 °C for varying durations up to 500 h in a controlled furnace.
measurements: Mass change (to quantify corrosion rate) at regular intervals.
High-magnification cross-sectional microscopy to assess coating integrity and substrate dissolution.
Physical testing (hardness or bend tests) to evaluate mechanical degradation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated boride specimens do not show both lower mass loss and superior mechanical integrity relative to the uncoated reference under these conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, a reinforced layer was prepared on the surface of HEA by powder-pack boriding and focused on the effect of temperature and duration on the boronizing of CoCrFeNiMn HEA. The boronized samples were characterized using various methods. Furthermore, the properties of boronized CoCrFeNiMn alloys and diffusion behavior were investigated. This study could provide a reference for high hardness and high wear resistance HEA that could be used in a variety of industrial applications, such as the mold and crucible used in the cast aluminum industry [,], because the borides formed on the surface have high hardness, excellent corrosion resistance, and wear resistance [,], which allow HEA to be applied in special environments to increase service life.

In addition, to obtain a uniform and stable protective layer, sputtering technology offers a fast deposition rate and a low-cost solution. Although the development of HEA systems has been going on for more than a decade, there are few reports on the deposition of stable protective films on HEA surfaces by conventional reactive sputtering techniques. Many studies have shown that sputter deposition of CrN film on conventional stainless steel is beneficial for its wear and corrosion resistance [,]. The CrN film deposited on the surface of 316 stainless steel has a positive effect on the friction behavior in NaCl solution and high temperature environments until heated to 550 °C []. In the tribo-corrosion test, the CrN coating layer can also remain relatively stable during the ball-on-plate sliding under various applied potentials []. As stainless steels are similar to CoCrNi-based MEAs in terms of their single FCC structure and lattice constant, this study attempts to sputter CrN film with a Cr buffer layer on the surface of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA and discusses in detail the improvement of corrosion and wear resistance of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA by sputtering CrN film.

decision.trend: Among the listed papers, only record PMC10221107 explicitly explores a boride-related surface modification (boronizing a high-entropy alloy). That study focused on improving wear resistance and hardness in a boronized CoCrFeNiMn surface but did not address molten aluminum corrosion. This reflects a broader trend in which researchers have pursued various thermochemical treatments (like boriding) or doping routes to enhance surface properties in high-entropy or complex alloys for corrosion or wear environments. However, direct tests against molten aluminum remain scarce, leaving the corrosion behavior of boride-based surfaces under hot-dip Al-plating conditions relatively unexplored.
decision.unsolved: While boriding and other surface treatments have improved hardness and wear resistance of certain alloys, the community still lacks definitive solutions for mitigating the aggressive attack of molten aluminum on boride-based components used in hot-dip plating. There is no clear consensus on which specific protective layer or interface architecture best resists liquid Al infiltration and dissolution over prolonged, high-temperature service.
decision.lever: Deposit a dense, thermally stable oxide overlayer (for example, a 1–2 µm Al2O3 coating via PVD or thermal spraying) to serve as a diffusion barrier between the boride substrate and molten aluminum. Key parameters include achieving near-complete coverage and controlling coating porosity below 1%.
decision.why: Building on prior success of boronized surface treatments (PMC10221107) and other surface modifications for corrosion/wear, the most logical step is to develop a robust, continuous oxide layer. Such a layer can prevent direct contact between molten Al and the boride phase, significantly limiting dissolution or interdiffusion and thereby improving corrosion resistance without resorting to bulk composition changes.
